title: Samantabhadra's promise (Kern ch. 26)
hookLine: the bodhisattva of practice promises to protect those who keep the sutra

lines: A LATE GUEST FROM THE EAST.
cards: The Lotus Sutra is nearly over when, in chapter twenty-six, a late guest arrives from a world far to the east, with a great company behind him. His name is Samantabhadra.
He bows and asks the Buddha a practical question, the kind someone asks near the end of a long meeting. After you are gone, how will people get hold of this teaching? What does it take?

teach.h: HOW TO GET HOLD OF THE TEACHING.
teach.b: The Buddha answers with a short list. Roughly: be held in the care of the Buddhas, plant roots of goodness, join the company of those set on the path, and turn the mind toward freeing all beings.
Then Samantabhadra makes his promise, and it's surprisingly concrete. Whoever keeps this sutra, he says, I will guard.

teach.h: A WHITE ELEPHANT WITH SIX TUSKS.
teach.b: When they walk and turn the teaching over in their mind, I'll come riding a white elephant with six tusks and stand before them. When they sit and reflect on it, I'll come again.

And if they forget a line, even one word, I'll be there to give it back. He adds protective spells, so nothing harmful can find an opening, and the Buddha praises him. Look at what the promise is attached to.
Not to being clever, not to being finished. To keeping: reading, remembering, turning the words over while walking.
The protection follows the practice, step for step. In the traditions that honor him, Samantabhadra is the bodhisattva of practice, of vows actually carried out.
It's the week's last day, so look back at the end of the Lotus. Spells to guard those who keep it. The Medicine King's offering.
Gadgadasvara in many forms. Guanyin hearing every cry, in a chapter chanted on its own.
Two sons leading a king. And now a bodhisattva on a white elephant. Week after week the Lotus has said: this is precious.
This week it added: you won't be left alone with it.

how: In East Asian Mahayana traditions Samantabhadra is honored as the bodhisattva of practice and vows, and temple images show him seated on a white elephant; communities that keep the Lotus Sutra read this chapter as his pledge to protect them.

games.q: you're Samantabhadra. the Lotus is almost done, and the Buddha won't be in the world forever. what do you offer?
o: to write the sutra's final chapter yourself.
to guard anyone who keeps it, and give back the lines they forget.
to carry the sutra away to a safer world.
games.why: he promises to come on a white elephant to whoever keeps the sutra, walking or sitting, and to restore any word they forget.

practice: Choose one small practice you already keep, or would like to: this sit, a line you say in the morning, a walk without your phone, watering a plant. Make it small enough to do tomorrow on a bad day.
Hold it the way you'd hold a promise to a friend, just for tomorrow, not forever.

wordCard.voice: Samantabhadra's promise. To come, on a white elephant, to anyone who keeps the sutra, and to give back any line they forget. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: the name of the bodhisattva who rides the white elephant in this chapter.

carryVoice: Your line: kept and protected. Even a forgotten line can be given back. That's the week, and nearly the whole Lotus.
